title: How Solar Panels Turn Sunlight Into Power
summary: Explains how solar panels catch sunlight and turn it into power, starting from a scientist's early clue that a certain metal could make power from light, through the first costly solar cell built in a research lab, to today's affordable solar panels found on rooftops, in solar farms, and even aboard space probes.
poll: Solar power will eventually become the main way most places in the world get their electricity.

versions.title: How Solar Panels Turn Sunlight Into Power
versions.text:
Solar panels catch light. The light is from the sun. They turn it into power. Many homes use them. This runs lights and tools.

A man once saw a strange thing. Light hit a bit of metal. The metal made some power. This was a clue. It helped folks later on.

Years on, folks made a cell. It was a solar cell. It was made in a lab. The lab was in the U.S. It could turn sunlight to power. But it cost too much.

Over time, workers got better. New cells cost far less. More folks could buy a few. Homes used them. Farms did too.

Solar panels sit on roofs. They stand in open fields. Some even fly in space. They work almost anywhere with sun.

Solar power helps our planet. It stays clean this way. It makes power with no coal. It makes power with no gas. More spots use it each year.

MID.prompt: Explain how solar power developed from an early scientific clue into a technology many people use today. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained how solar power developed.
I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Solar power developed slowly, starting with a scientist who noticed that light hitting a certain kind of metal produced a tiny amount of power. This small discovery mattered a great deal to later inventors and researchers, who eventually built the first practical solar cell in a research laboratory in the United States. At first, this solar cell cost far too much money for most people to use. Over time, engineers became much better at manufacturing solar cells, so the cost dropped and more ordinary families and farms could finally afford them. Today, solar panels sit on countless rooftops, stand together in large solar farms, and even travel aboard space probes exploring distant parts of space.

HIGH.prompt: The article suggests that solar power only became truly transformative once engineers made it efficient and affordable for ordinary households, long after the original scientific discovery. Do you think the technical, unglamorous work of making an invention affordable is as important as the original scientific discovery itself? Support your answer with evidence from the article, and address at least one point someone might raise against your view.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the question.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one counterpoint.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think the technical, unglamorous work of making an invention affordable is just as important as the original scientific discovery, based on the evidence in this article. The article shows that a scientist's early observation about light and metal was a meaningful clue, but it took decades of careful manufacturing improvements by engineers before solar panels became something ordinary households and farms could actually afford. Someone might argue that the original discovery deserves more credit, since without it there would be nothing for engineers to improve in the first place. That is a reasonable point to consider. However, the article shows that the first practical solar cell, despite being a real scientific achievement, remained mostly unused because it cost far too much money, which suggests that the technical work of lowering costs was what truly allowed solar power to transform how households, farms, and even space missions get their electricity.
